content: The studies reviewed here provide evidence on the effectiveness of various interventions aimed at improving maternal and newborn health outcomes, particularly in relation to skilled birth attendance (SBA), antenatal care (ANC), and postnatal care (PNC). 1. Births with Skilled Birth Attendants (SBAs) or Facility Births: Six observational studies were analyzed, with two rated as having moderate methodological quality and four as weak. The evidence was deemed to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. The studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, with two focusing exclusively on refugee or internally displaced women. The interventions were complex and multifaceted, making it difficult to isolate the effects of individual components or distinguish them from existing safe motherhood initiatives. Preand post-intervention studies lacked concurrent control groups, limiting their ability to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of traditional birth attendant (TBA) interventions in improving SBA rates. Five studies reported on SBA use, but definitions of SBA were inconsistent. Two studies reported facility births, and the two studies rated as moderate showed a trend of increased SBA use over time. Among studies with high risk of bias, two indicated an increase in SBA use (one significantly), while one suggested fewer women exposed to the intervention had SBA. Facility births increased over time in one study involving emergency obstetric care (EmOC) provision in a refugee population and in another study using a culturally adapted childbirth model. 2. Use of Antenatal Care (ANC): Three observational studies were reviewed, with two rated as moderate quality and one as weak. The evidence was considered to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. The studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, with two focusing on refugee or internally displaced women. The interventions were complex and varied, making it challenging to attribute outcomes to specific components. All three studies reported an increase in ANC use over time, with larger improvements observed following the implementation of TBA interventions in settings with refugee and internally displaced women. 3. Postnatal Care (PNC) Visits: Four observational studies were analyzed, with three rated as weak and one as moderate quality. The evidence was deemed to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. Two studies were conducted in low-income and two in middle-income countries, with two focusing on refugee or internally displaced women. The interventions were complex and multifaceted, making it difficult to isolate the effects of individual components. All four studies reported an increase in PNC visits over time, with larger relative improvements observed following the implementation of TBA interventions in settings with refugee and internally displaced women. 4. Culturally Appropriate Skilled Maternity Care: Two observational studies of weak methodological quality were reviewed. The evidence was considered to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. One study was conducted in a high-income country, and the other in a middle-income country. The interventions differed, with one focusing on culturally appropriate delivery care and the other on antenatal care. Both studies reported facility births, and one also reported on SBA use. The new delivery care model resulted in increased births with SBAs and facility births over time, but the lack of control groups means other factors could have influenced the outcomes. 5. Care with Skilled Birth Attendants or Facility Births in Cases of Maternal Complications/Illness: Two observational studies of moderate quality were reviewed. The evidence was considered to have a serious risk of bias and indirectness. Both studies were conducted in high-income countries, but the populations and interventions differed. One study focused on high-risk, low-income Mexican-American women in the USA, while the other involved Turkish and Asian women in the UK. Both studies reported antenatal admissions and length of stay but did not provide data on SBA use in cases of maternal complications. Results differed across the studies, with one showing a significant effect of health advocates on length of stay, while the other found no difference. 6. Use of ANC (1 or 4 Visits): Eleven observational studies were reviewed, with eight rated as weak and three as moderate quality. The evidence was deemed to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. All studies were conducted in high-income countries with ethnic minority women. The interventions were culturally appropriate and multifaceted, making them difficult to replicate and challenging to attribute outcomes to specific components. Eight studies showed a greater number of ANC visits among women receiving interventions designed to improve culturally appropriate skilled maternity care, while three studies were unclear on the benefit. Three studies reported more adequate ANC use among women receiving the intervention. 7. Postpartum Care Visit (Mother): One randomized control study of weak methodological quality was reviewed. The evidence was considered to have a very serious risk of bias and indirectness. The study involved low-income Latina/Hispanic pregnant women in the USA. The intervention was based on cultural brokers providing educational and support services, which were multifaceted and likely difficult to replicate. The study reported compliance with the 6–8 week postpartum visit, with women in the intervention group being five times more likely to attend. However, the study design flaws necessitate cautious interpretation of the findings. In summary, while the reviewed studies suggest some positive trends in improving maternal and newborn health outcomes through various interventions, the evidence is limited by methodological weaknesses, lack of control groups, and challenges in isolating the effects of specific intervention components.
